```{r setup}
suppressPackageStartupMessages({

})

# The analysis frame, the prior specifications and the derived-quantity
# functions come from the report context the pipeline builds; the fits come
# from the targets store.  Nothing here samples and there is no cache
# directory to point at: run tar_make() and every fit this document reads is
# current with the data and the code by construction.
tar_load(c(ctx_report, barg_mf, ppc_stat_tbl, barg_figs,
           fit_ref, fit_prior_ref, fit_noland, fit_ref_rg_ln, fit_ref_basinx))

# Copying the context in gives this document the same names the scripts used
# to define by being sourced here -- resps, link_sd, ROPE_SD, coef_table(),
# icc_table() and the rest -- so the 2000 lines below are unchanged.  The two
# manuscript documents cannot do this, because barg_data.R and _analysis.R use
# some of the same names for different things; they keep the ctx- prefix.
list2env(as.list(ctx_report, all.names = TRUE), envir = globalenv())

# The six S-fits and the two variants are read one at a time, so that the
# render never holds more than two large fits in memory.  They are named in
# the tar_load() below purely so that tar_quarto() sees them as dependencies
# of this document; the call is never evaluated.
if (FALSE) tar_load(c(fit_s1, fit_s2, fit_s3, fit_s4, fit_s5, fit_s6))
gf  <- function(n) targets::tar_read_raw(paste0("fit_", n))
FIG <- function(n) here("paper", "barg", "figures", n)

fit_prior <- fit_prior_ref
mf <- barg_mf

# ---- everything the text and the tables quote ---------------------------
cf       <- coef_table(fit_ref)
icc_ref  <- icc_table(fit_ref)
icc_nol  <- icc_table(fit_noland)
cor_tb   <- cor_table(fit_ref)
ppsd_ref <- prior_post_sd(fit_ref, fit_prior)

# The six S-fits are large.  They are loaded one at a time, reduced
# to the quantities the report needs, and dropped again, so that the render
# never holds more than two fits in memory at once.
SENS <- c(REF = "ref", S1 = "s1", S2 = "s2", S3 = "s3", S4 = "s4", S5 = "s5",
          S6 = "s6")
ppsd_s1  <- NULL
sens_long <- bind_rows(lapply(names(SENS), function(nm) {
  if (nm == "REF") {
    d <- as_draws_df(fit_ref)
  } else {
    f <- gf(SENS[[nm]])
    if (nm == "S1")
      ppsd_s1 <<- prior_post_sd(f, NULL, b_sd = setNames(rep(1, 7), resps))
    d <- as_draws_df(f); rm(f); gc()
  }
  out <- bind_rows(
    bind_rows(lapply(resps, function(r) {
      x <- icc_draws(d, r, resp_fam[[r]]); q <- eti(x)
      data.frame(Spec = nm, Quantity = paste0("ICC: ", unname(resp_lab[r])),
                 Median = median(x), lo = q[1], hi = q[2],
                 inrope = mean(x <= ICC_ROPE))
    })),
    bind_rows(lapply(resps, function(r) bind_rows(lapply(preds, function(pp) {
      x <- d[[paste0("b_", r, "_", pp)]] / link_sd[[r]]; q <- eti(x)
      data.frame(Spec = nm,
                 Quantity = paste0(unname(resp_lab[r]), " ~ ", unname(pred_lab[pp])),
                 Median = median(x), lo = q[1], hi = q[2],
                 inrope = mean(abs(x) < ROPE_SD))
    })))))
  rm(d); gc(); out
}))

dr_ref <- as_draws_df(fit_ref)
sm_ref <- summarise_draws(dr_ref, "rhat", "ess_bulk", "ess_tail")
sm_ref <- sm_ref[!is.na(sm_ref$rhat) & !startsWith(sm_ref$variable, "lp"), ]
np_ref <- nuts_params(fit_ref)
n_div  <- sum(np_ref$Value[np_ref$Parameter == "divergent__"])
n_tree <- sum(np_ref$Value[np_ref$Parameter == "treedepth__"] >= 10)

fmt  <- function(x, d = 2) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d)
ci   <- function(m, l, h, d = 3) sprintf("%s [%s, %s]", fmt(m, d), fmt(l, d), fmt(h, d))
kt   <- function(x, caption, digits = 3, ...)
  knitr::kable(x, caption = caption, digits = digits, row.names = FALSE, ...)
rlab <- function(x) unname(resp_lab[x])
plab <- function(x) unname(pred_lab[x])
```

```{r}
icc_dec <- icc_ref |> arrange(desc(Median))
present <- icc_dec |> filter(Verdict == "locality variation present")
undec   <- icc_dec |> filter(Verdict == "undecided")
icc_j <- icc_ref |> select(Response, ref = Median, ref_lo = CrI_lo) |>
  left_join(icc_nol |> select(Response, nol = Median), by = "Response") |>
  mutate(change = ref - nol, rel = change / nol)   # positive = ICC rose

# how the Q1 decision behaves across the seven priors
icc_sens <- sens_long |>
  filter(startsWith(Quantity, "ICC: ")) |>
  mutate(Resp = sub("^ICC: ", "", Quantity),
         dec = ifelse(lo > ICC_ROPE, "present",
               ifelse(hi < ICC_ROPE, "negligible", "undecided")))
icc_stable <- icc_sens |> group_by(Resp) |>
  summarise(k = n_distinct(dec), ref = dec[Spec == "REF"], .groups = "drop")
firm  <- icc_stable |> filter(k == 1, ref == "present")
flips <- icc_stable |> filter(k > 1)
flip_detail <- icc_sens |> semi_join(flips, by = "Resp") |> filter(dec != "present")
```

```{r}
sens_verdict <- sens_long |>
  mutate(is_icc = startsWith(Quantity, "ICC: "),
         Decision = ifelse(is_icc,
           ifelse(lo > ICC_ROPE, "locality variation present",
             ifelse(hi < ICC_ROPE, "negligible", "undecided")),
           rope_verdict(lo, hi, 100 * inrope, ROPE_SD))) |>

changed <- sens_verdict |>
  rowwise() |>
  mutate(n_distinct_dec = n_distinct(c_across(all_of(names(SENS))))) |>
```

```{r}
#| label: s6-identity
#| echo: false
# S6, the one-inflated refit.  coef_table() and icc_table() carry the median
# and its Monte Carlo standard error, so the comparison with the reference can
# be made in MCSE units: if the two posteriors are the same distribution, their
# medians should differ by a couple of MCSEs and by nothing more.  The fit is
# loaded once here, reduced, and dropped.
s6_q <- local({
  f <- gf("s6")
  out <- list(cf = coef_table(f), icc = icc_table(f))
  rm(f); gc(); out
})

s6_id <- cf |>
  select(Response, Predictor, ref_med = Median, ref_mcse = MCSE_med,
         ref_sd = SD, ref_v = Verdict) |>
  left_join(s6_q$cf |> select(Response, Predictor, s6_med = Median,
                              s6_mcse = MCSE_med, s6_v = Verdict),
            by = c("Response", "Predictor")) |>
  mutate(d = s6_med - ref_med,
         mcse_pair = sqrt(ref_mcse^2 + s6_mcse^2),
         z = abs(d) / mcse_pair,
         rel_sd = abs(d) / ref_sd)

s6_icc_id <- icc_ref |>
  select(Response, ref_med = Median, ref_mcse = MCSE_med, ref_sd = SD,
         ref_v = Verdict) |>
  left_join(s6_q$icc |> select(Response, s6_med = Median, s6_mcse = MCSE_med,
                               s6_v = Verdict),
            by = "Response") |>
  mutate(d = s6_med - ref_med,
         z = abs(d) / sqrt(ref_mcse^2 + s6_mcse^2),
         rel_sd = abs(d) / ref_sd)

# every decision the report draws, under both specifications
s6_same_slope <- all(s6_id$ref_v == s6_id$s6_v)
s6_same_icc   <- all(s6_icc_id$ref_v == s6_icc_id$s6_v)

# what the reference fit's own coi implies: a probability of an exact zero,
# and an expected count of zeros, in a sample that contains none
coi_ref  <- dr_ref[["coi_GIUR"]]
zoi_ref  <- dr_ref[["zoi_GIUR"]]
p0_ref   <- zoi_ref * (1 - coi_ref)
n0_exp   <- median(p0_ref) * n_spec
```

# Summary {#sec-summary}

## What this document is

This is Supplementary material 2, the statistical supplement to the main paper. It reports one Bayesian
analysis in full: the data, the model, the priors, the computation, the
posterior, the decisions drawn from it, and how far those decisions depend on
choices that could have been made differently. The reporting follows the
Bayesian Analysis Reporting Guidelines of Kruschke (2021), and @sec-barg maps
every item of that checklist onto the section that answers it. The main
narrative, @sec-analysis to @sec-reproducibility, is written to be read
straight through; the appendices hold the complete tables, the model code and
the diagnostics. A reader who wants the vocabulary first will find it in
@sec-reading-guide.

## What was analysed

`r n_spec` surface-collected Quina scrapers from `r n_loc` localities in two
basins, Binchuan and Huangping. Seven measurements were taken on each
specimen: its thickness, its overall size, its GIUR, the retouched share of
its perimeter, its total scar count, its edge angle, and the number of retouch
generations it carries. Three further attributes describe the locality rather
than the specimen: which basin it lies in, how high it sits above the channel,
and how far it is from the channel. Each is the same for every specimen
collected from that locality.

All seven measurements were fitted in a single model, so that one locality
structure is shared across them rather than seven separate analyses being run
and compared afterwards. The model gives every locality its own level for
every measurement, and estimates two things: how much of the variation in each
measurement sits between localities rather than between specimens, and how
much of that the three landscape attributes account for.

## What was found

### Q1: do the localities differ from one another?

Yes, for `r nrow(present)` of the seven measurements ---
`r paste(rlab(present$Response), collapse = ", ")`. Between
`r fmt(min(present$Median) * 100, 0)`% and
`r fmt(max(present$Median) * 100, 0)`% of the variation in those measures sits
between localities rather than between specimens within a locality. For
`r nrow(firm)` of the seven measures the finding survives every one of the prior
settings the model was refitted under, which is the stronger and safer
reading (@sec-q1). The remaining `r nrow(undec)` measures are undecided: the
data are compatible both with substantial differences between localities and
with none.

### Q2: do basin, elevation or distance to the channel explain the differences?

No. Of the `r nrow(cf)` landscape effects estimated, `r n_rej` are large
enough for the analysis to call them real, `r n_acc` small enough for it to
call them practically absent, and `r n_und` fall between the two. A more
direct piece of evidence points the same way: adding all three landscape
attributes to a model that lacks them barely moves the share of variation
sitting between localities, the median change across the seven measures being
`r sprintf("%+.1f", med_rel * 100)`% (@sec-q1).

An undecided verdict is not an empty result, and it is where this study is
most informative. For each landscape effect there is a smallest size the data
can rule out, and translating it into the measurement's own units makes it
concrete. For the three best-resolved effects the study rules out anything
larger than
`r paste(sprintf("%s with %s, +/- %s %s", rlab(best$Response), tolower(plab(best$Predictor)), fmt(abs(best$Min_ROPE_resp), 0), best$Min_ROPE_unit), collapse = "; ")`.
@tbl-min-rope gives the same bound for all `r nrow(cf)` effects, in degrees,
in generations, and in percentage changes of the measurement.

## What the study cannot settle

Three limits matter more than any single number above.

The landscape questions are answered by `r n_loc` localities, not by
`r n_spec` specimens. All three landscape attributes are constant within a
locality, so collecting more scrapers from the localities already sampled
would sharpen the description of those localities without sharpening the
answer to Q2.

The basin comparison is a single contrast, between
`r sum(tapply(as.character(mod_dat$Basin), mod_dat$Locality, function(x) x[1]) == "Binchuan")`
localities and
`r sum(tapply(as.character(mod_dat$Basin), mod_dat$Locality, function(x) x[1]) == "Huangping")`.
Whatever separates the two basins, this design compares two groups of
localities once, and the width of that comparison's interval reflects it.

The assemblages are very unequal. One locality supplies
`r max(table(mod_dat$Locality))` of the `r n_spec` specimens while
`r sum(table(mod_dat$Locality) == 1)` localities supply a single specimen
each. The model borrows strength across localities so that the small ones are
not read as well-measured, but it cannot supply information the sample does
not contain.

@sec-resolution-limits states these three limits precisely and adds three
more that bear on particular measures.

# BARG conformance {#sec-barg}

Kruschke (2021) sets out a checklist for reporting a Bayesian analysis. Every
item on it is listed below against the section that answers it. The same
checklist can be walked from the other direction: each section of this
document opens with a shaded box naming the item it addresses.

| BARG item | How it is addressed | Where |
|---|---|---|
| **Preamble A.** Why a Bayesian approach is used | Seven responses on three link scales share one locality-level structure in a single model; derived quantities carry genuine intervals; a null value can be accepted rather than merely not rejected; no large-sample approximation is needed in a design with few clusters | @sec-why-bayes |
| **Preamble B.** The goals of the analysis | Estimation of each landscape effect and of the locality variance, and decisions about null values. Prediction and model comparison are not goals | @sec-goals |
| **1.A.** Data variables, their roles and types | Seven responses, three locality-level predictors, one grouping factor, with the observed range of each; the complete-case filter is audited step by step | @sec-data, @tbl-data-vars, @tbl-dropped |
| **1.B.** The likelihood and its parameters, separating those of theoretical interest from nuisance parameters | One multivariate model over four distributional families, with the linear predictor written out; the slopes and the locality SDs answer the questions, the intercepts, dispersion parameters and 21 correlations do not | @sec-likelihood, @tbl-likelihood |
| **1.C.** The prior distribution and its justification | Every class given an explicit prior, the slope prior scaled to each response's own link-scale SD, with the share of prior mass inside each response's ROPE as the argument for scaling it | @sec-priors, @sec-priors-full |
| **1.D.** Formal specification of the model | The brms formula and the complete generated Stan program | @sec-formal |
| **1.E.** Prior predictive check | The reference prior refitted with `sample_prior = "only"`, and the simulated data checked against the physically possible range of each measure | @sec-prior-pred, @tbl-prior-pred |
| **2.A.** Software, versions and settings | R, brms, backend and CmdStan versions, chains, iterations, warmup, seed, `adapt_delta` and `max_treedepth`, for all eleven runs | @sec-software, @tbl-software |
| **2.B.** MCMC chain convergence | R-hat, divergent transitions and treedepth saturation, for the reference fit and for all eleven runs | @sec-convergence, @tbl-diag-all |
| **2.C.** MCMC chain resolution | Bulk and tail effective sample size for every parameter and every derived ICC, with the Monte Carlo standard error of each quantile the report actually quotes | @sec-resolution, @tbl-convergence |
| **2.D.** Accuracy of any approximation used in place of exact sampling | Not applicable: every posterior in this document is a full MCMC sample, with no variational, Laplace or INLA approximation anywhere | --- |
| **3.A.** Posterior predictive check | Full predictive distributions, checks by basin and by locality, and test statistics fixed in advance | @sec-post-pred, @sec-ppc-stats, @tbl-ppc-stats |
| **3.B.** Summary of the posterior of every parameter | Posterior median and 95% equal-tailed interval, with mode and 95% HDI alongside, for the 21 slopes, the seven locality SDs and ICCs, and the 21 correlations | @sec-posterior-summary, @sec-icc, @sec-cor |
| **3.C.** Bayes factors and posterior model probabilities | Not applicable: no model comparison is performed, so no marginal likelihood, no bridge sampling and no Bayes factor appears anywhere in this document | Not applicable (@sec-goals) |
| **4.A.** The decision procedure and its rule | Kruschke's (2018) three-way decision --- reject, accept, undecided --- against a region of practical equivalence | @sec-decision-rule |
| **4.B.** The loss or utility function, where decisions are made by formal decision theory | Not applicable: no cost attaches to being wrong about a landscape slope, so no loss function is specified; the ROPE curve reports the whole family of decisions instead of committing to one | Not applicable (@sec-rope) |
| **4.C.** ROPE limits and their justification | Half-width 0.1 of each response's link-scale SD, with the convention acknowledged and the posterior mass reported as a continuous function of the half-width | @sec-rope, @fig-rope |
| **4.D.** Bayes-factor decision thresholds | Not applicable: no Bayes factor is used, so no threshold on one is needed | Not applicable (@sec-goals) |
| **4.E.** Each decision reported with the estimate and interval it rests on | Every decision table carries the median, the 95% interval, the posterior mass inside the ROPE and the verdict in the same row | @sec-q1, @sec-q2 |
| **5.A.** Sensitivity to a broad prior | S2 widens every slope prior by a factor of 2.5; S3, S4 and S5 do the same job for the locality SD and for the correlation matrix | @sec-5a, @tbl-sens-specs |
| **5.B.** Sensitivity to a genuinely informed prior drawn from previous research | Not applicable: no published posterior or meta-analytic estimate exists for any of these seven measures in Quina assemblages, so no informed prior can be built; the gap is discussed where the priors are set out | Not applicable (@sec-priors) |
| **5.C.** Variations of the default priors | Six fits, each differing from the reference in exactly one prior, with every ICC and every slope reported under all seven specifications | @sec-5c, @tbl-sens-full |
| **5.D.** Sensitivity of the Bayes factor to the prior | Not applicable: no Bayes factor is computed. The item is singled out in the guideline because Bayes factors are prior-dependent in a way posterior estimates are not, which is part of why this analysis is framed as estimation | Not applicable (@sec-goals) |
| **5.E.** Whether the conclusions change | The decision each quantity receives under each of the seven priors, and the largest movement of a posterior median relative to that quantity's own interval width; and, for the one structural question the design can pose, whether the landscape slopes differ between the two basins | @sec-prior-dependence, @sec-basinx, @sec-5e |
| **6.** Reproducibility of data, code and computational environment | Software versions, the file list, the archive DOI, a synthetic dataset for the case where the specimens cannot be released, run instructions and `sessionInfo()` | @sec-reproducibility |

# Reading guide {#sec-reading-guide}

Ten terms carry most of the technical weight of what follows. Each is glossed
again, in one clause, where it first appears in the main narrative.

| Term | What it means here |
|---|---|
| Posterior distribution | The distribution of a quantity --- a slope, a share of variance --- after the data have been combined with the prior. Every number in this document is a summary of one. |
| 95% credible interval | The central range holding 95% of the posterior. It says where the quantity lies, given this model and these data. A confidence interval says something different: it describes the long-run behaviour of the procedure that produced it, not the quantity. |
| ROPE | Region of practical equivalence: the band of values around zero that the analysis is willing to treat as no effect. Calling an effect absent means showing that the posterior sits inside that band. |
| Intraclass correlation (ICC) | The share of a measure's variation that sits between localities rather than between specimens within a locality. |
| Link scale, and dividing by the link-scale SD | Thickness is modelled on a logarithmic scale, GIUR on a log-odds scale, edge angle in degrees. A slope on one of those scales cannot be compared with a slope on another until each is divided by the spread of its own response on its own scale. Every standardised slope here has been divided in that way, which is what lets one ROPE serve all seven measures. |
| Partial pooling | A locality with one specimen is estimated partly from the other localities, so its level is pulled towards the overall level. It stops a single-specimen locality from being read as a well-measured one. |
| Prior predictive check | Simulating data from the prior alone, before the real data are used, to confirm that the prior puts no weight on physically impossible values. |
| Posterior predictive check | Simulating data from the fitted model and comparing them with the observed data, to see what the model reproduces and what it misses. |
| R-hat and effective sample size | Diagnostics of the simulation rather than of the archaeology. R-hat near 1 means the independently started chains agree; the effective sample size says how many independent draws the correlated ones are worth. |
| Sensitivity analysis | Refitting under different priors to find out which conclusions depend on the prior and which do not. |

---

# The analysis {#sec-analysis}

## Why the analysis is Bayesian {#sec-why-bayes}

::: {.barg}
Cf. BARG Preamble A.
:::

Four considerations led to a Bayesian treatment.

The seven measures on a Quina scraper are not on one scale. Thickness and
overall size are positive and right-skewed; the geometric index of unifacial
reduction (GIUR) and the retouched share of the perimeter are proportions with
mass piled at one; the scar count is a count; the edge angle and the number of
retouch generations are treated as unbounded. A single multivariate model that
gives each measure the likelihood its scale calls for, and still shares one
locality-level random structure across all seven, is straightforward to write
down and fit by MCMC, and awkward to fit any other way.

The quantity that answers the first research question is the share of
link-scale variance attributable to locality, an intraclass correlation built
from a variance component and a residual variance that are themselves
functions of several parameters. Under MCMC it is computed draw by draw and
inherits a genuine interval, with no approximation and no delta-method step.

The substantive claim under test is that the landscape variables do *not*
explain the between-locality differences. A frequentist test can only fail to
reject that. A posterior distribution combined with a region of practical
equivalence can accept it, reject it, or report that the data do not decide
(@sec-decision-rule).

The design has $n = `r n_spec`$ specimens but only $`r n_loc`$ localities, and
every predictor is a locality-level attribute (@sec-data). Asymptotic
intervals for the variance component of a `r n_loc`-cluster design are not to
be trusted; posterior intervals require no such argument.

## Goals and the two research questions {#sec-goals}

::: {.barg}
Cf. BARG Preamble B.
:::

The goals are two. The first is estimation: the magnitude of each landscape
effect and of the locality-level variance, with uncertainty. The second is
decision about null values, meaning whether each landscape effect is small
enough to be treated as absent.
Prediction of new specimens is not a goal. Formal model selection is not a
goal either: there is one model here and its coefficients are being estimated,
rather than a set of competing scientific hypotheses being weighed against
each other. The reference BARG example marks the same boundary: where the
goal is estimation rather than model comparison, the analysis is complete
once the posterior and its sensitivity have been reported.

Q1 asks whether there is technological variation between localities at all. It
is answered by the locality variance component and the intraclass correlation
it implies --- the share of a measure's variation that sits between localities
rather than between specimens within a locality (@sec-icc, @sec-q1).

Q2 asks whether that variation can be explained by basin, elevation above the
channel, or distance to the channel. It is answered by the population-level
slopes (@sec-posterior-summary, @sec-q2).

The two are asked in that order for a reason. If there is nothing to explain,
the second question has no content; and if Q1 is answered yes while Q2 returns
"the data do not say", those are two different results and should not be
merged into one.

## Data {#sec-data}

::: {.barg}
Cf. BARG Step 1.A.
:::

```{r}
#| label: tbl-data-vars
kt(data.frame(
  Variable = c(rlab(resps), "Basin", "Height above channel", "Distance to channel",
               "Locality"),
  Role = c(rep("response", 7), rep("predictor (locality level)", 3), "grouping factor"),
  Type = c("continuous, positive (mm)",
           "continuous, positive (mm); geometric mean of length, width and thickness",
           "proportion in [0, 1]", "proportion in [0, 1]", "count",
           "continuous (degrees)", "continuous (generations)",
           "binary: Binchuan / Huangping", "continuous (m)", "continuous (m)",
           "factor, 26 levels"),
  Observed = c(
    sprintf("%.1f - %.1f", sapply(resps, function(r) min(mod_dat[[r]])),
                            sapply(resps, function(r) max(mod_dat[[r]]))),
    sprintf("%d / %d", sum(mod_dat$Basin == "Binchuan"), sum(mod_dat$Basin == "Huangping")),
    sprintf("%.0f - %.0f", min(mod_dat$Height), max(mod_dat$Height)),
    sprintf("%.0f - %.0f", min(mod_dat$Distance), max(mod_dat$Distance)),
    sprintf("%d specimens in %d localities", n_spec, n_loc))),
  caption = "The variables entering the model, and their observed range in the analysed sample.")
```

`GMsize` is the geometric mean of the three linear dimensions,
$$\mathrm{GMsize} = (\mathrm{Length}\times\mathrm{Width}\times\mathrm{Thickness})^{1/3},$$
computed for each specimen. The definition lives in the analysis code rather
than in any measurement protocol, and it is stated here because it has a
consequence.

Thickness is one of the three factors in GMsize, so the two responses share a
component before any archaeology enters. The model is fitted with
`set_rescor(FALSE)`, which assumes the *residuals* of the seven responses are
independent given the locality intercepts, and that assumption is not credible
for this pair. The practical consequence is confined. With `rescor = FALSE`
the multivariate model factorises into seven univariate models sharing only
the correlated random intercepts, so the slopes and their intervals for each
response remain valid marginally. What is not valid is any statement about the
*joint* uncertainty of, say, the thickness slope and the size slope, or any
reading of the two as independent evidence. The observed correlation between
the locality intercepts of the two (@sec-cor) should therefore be read as
partly mechanical.

Two filters were applied before fitting. A specimen must carry all seven
measurements, and its locality must have a recorded basin, height and
distance.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-dropped
kt(drop_log |> mutate(lost = c(NA, diff(n))) |>
     rename(`specimens remaining` = n, `lost at this step` = lost),
   caption = "Complete-case filtering. One specimen was dropped, for a missing GIUR.",
   digits = 0)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-localities
kt(mod_dat |> count(Basin, Locality) |> count(Basin, name = "localities") |>
     left_join(mod_dat |> count(Basin, name = "specimens"), by = "Basin") |>
     mutate(`specimens per locality` = sprintf("%d - %d",
       tapply(mod_dat$Locality, mod_dat$Basin, function(x) min(table(droplevels(x)))),
       tapply(mod_dat$Locality, mod_dat$Basin, function(x) max(table(droplevels(x)))))),
   caption = "Localities and specimens by basin. Heqing, which appears under that name in the site table, is folded into Huangping: the two names refer to the same basin.",
   digits = 0)
```

The specimen count overstates what the design carries for Q2. All three
predictors --- basin, height above the channel, distance to the channel --- are
constant within a locality, so for the population-level slopes the design
carries close to `r n_loc` independent units rather than `r n_spec`, and the
`r n_loc` are unevenly filled: the largest locality contributes
`r max(table(mod_dat$Locality))` specimens and
`r sum(table(mod_dat$Locality) == 1)` localities contribute one each. Basin is
worse still, being a single binary contrast between
`r sum(tapply(as.character(mod_dat$Basin), mod_dat$Locality, function(x) x[1]) == "Binchuan")`
and
`r sum(tapply(as.character(mod_dat$Basin), mod_dat$Locality, function(x) x[1]) == "Huangping")`
localities. The random intercept is what keeps the specimen count from being
read as `r n_spec` independent observations of the landscape effects, and it
is why the intervals in @sec-posterior-summary are as wide as they are.

The standardisation is specimen-weighted: `zHeight` and `zDistance` are
centred and scaled over the `r n_spec` specimens rather than over the
`r n_loc` localities, so a locality enters the centring and the scaling with
the weight of its own assemblage. A locality-weighted standardisation would
give slightly different numerical slopes on a rescaled axis. It would not
change any decision, because every slope is reported divided by the link-scale
SD of its own response and the ROPE moves with it.

## Model and likelihoods {#sec-likelihood}

::: {.barg}
Cf. BARG Step 1.B.
:::

For specimen $i$ in locality $j$, each response $r$ has its own likelihood
with a linear predictor on its own link scale:

$$
g_r(\mu^{(r)}_{ij}) \;=\; \beta^{(r)}_{0} \;+\; \beta^{(r)}_{\text{Basin}}\,\mathrm{Basin}_j
\;+\; \beta^{(r)}_{\text{H}}\,\mathrm{zHeight}_j
\;+\; \beta^{(r)}_{\text{D}}\,\mathrm{zDistance}_j \;+\; u^{(r)}_j ,
$$

$$
\bigl(u^{(1)}_j,\dots,u^{(7)}_j\bigr)^{\!\top} \sim
\mathrm{MVNormal}\bigl(\mathbf 0,\;\mathbf D\,\boldsymbol\Omega\,\mathbf D\bigr),
\qquad \mathbf D=\mathrm{diag}(\sigma^{(1)}_u,\dots,\sigma^{(7)}_u).
$$

```{r}
#| label: tbl-likelihood
kt(data.frame(
  Response = rlab(resps),
  Likelihood = unname(fam_lab[resp_fam]),
  `Link for the mean` = unname(link_lab[resp_fam]),
  `Auxiliary parameters` = c("sigma", "sigma", "phi, zoi, coi", "phi, zoi, coi",
                             "shape", "sigma", "sigma"),
  `Link-scale SD` = round(link_sd, 3), check.names = FALSE),
  caption = "Likelihoods. The last column is the SD of the observed response on its own link scale; it is the unit in which every slope and every ROPE below is expressed.")
```

### Parameters of theoretical interest and nuisance parameters

Of the `r nrow(sm_ref)` estimated parameters, the ones the research questions
are about are the `r nrow(cf)` population-level slopes
$\beta^{(r)}_{\text{Basin}}, \beta^{(r)}_{\text{H}}, \beta^{(r)}_{\text{D}}$
(Q2) and the seven locality SDs $\sigma^{(r)}_u$ together with the ICCs
derived from them (Q1). The seven intercepts, the auxiliary parameters
(`sigma`, `phi`, `shape`, `zoi`, `coi`) and the 21 elements of
$\boldsymbol\Omega$ are needed to make the model coherent but carry no
hypothesis. The correlations are nevertheless reported in full (@sec-cor),
because they were estimated and BARG asks for every parameter of the model to
be described.

With `r sum(table(mod_dat$Locality) == 1)` localities of one specimen, the
locality offsets are strongly shrunk towards the grand mean. That shrinkage is
partial pooling: a locality with little data of its own is estimated partly
from the others, and the caterpillar plot in @sec-cor shows how far each is
pulled. It is the intended behaviour, and it is why the ICC is computed from
the fitted variance components rather than from a between-group variance ratio
of raw locality means.

### A trap in the zero-one-inflated beta parameterisation

For GIUR and the retouched perimeter, the three predictors enter only the beta
component's mean `mu`. The inflation parameters `zoi` (the probability that a
value is exactly 0 or exactly 1) and `coi` (the probability that such a value
is 1 rather than 0) are pure intercepts, constant across basins, elevations
and distances. Two consequences follow for every GIUR and RLI number in this
report.

1. A reported slope is the effect on the **logit of the beta-component mean,
   conditional on the value lying strictly inside (0, 1)**. It is not the
   effect on the unconditional expected GIUR, which also moves with `zoi` and
   `coi`.
2. The ICC for these two responses is likewise computed from the beta
   component alone and ignores the inflation entirely.

In this sample there are `r sum(mod_dat$GIUR == 1)` specimens with GIUR
exactly 1 and `r sum(mod_dat$GIUR == 0)` with GIUR exactly 0, and
`r sum(mod_dat$RLI == 1)` and `r sum(mod_dat$RLI == 0)` for the retouched
perimeter. There is therefore no zero inflation at all to model: the fitted
`coi` is a posterior over "all inflated values are ones", which the data
determine almost completely, and the zero-inflation half of the family is
supported by nothing. The family is effectively a one-inflated beta.

### S6, the one-inflated refit {#sec-oneinflated}

The paragraph above describes a defect rather than a design choice, and S6 acts
on it. `coi` is fixed at 1 --- `constant(1)` in `barg_priors.R` --- which makes
the family the one-inflated beta the data actually describe: mass at 1, none at
0, and the zero-inflation half that nothing supports removed rather than
estimated. brms implements the constant by moving `coi_GIUR` and `coi_RLI` out
of the Stan `parameters` block into `transformed parameters`, so two parameters
genuinely leave the sampled space rather than being given a tight prior. The
change is visible in @tbl-diag-all, where S6 is estimated over
`r mf$diagnostics$n_par[mf$diagnostics$fit == "s6"]` parameters against
`r mf$diagnostics$n_par[mf$diagnostics$fit == "ref"]` for the reference and
every other prior specification.

The reference fit shows why this is worth doing. Under `beta(1, 1)` and
`r sum(mod_dat$GIUR == 1)` ones out of `r n_spec` specimens, the posterior for
GIUR's `coi` is centred at `r fmt(median(coi_ref), 3)` rather than at 1, so the
reference model holds back
`r fmt(100 * (1 - median(coi_ref)), 1)`% of the inflation mass for an outcome
that cannot occur. Multiplied through by `zoi`, it puts the probability of an
exact zero at `r fmt(median(p0_ref), 4)` and expects
**`r fmt(n0_exp, 2)`** zeros among the `r n_spec` specimens, where the data
contain none. The misfit is small, but it is a misfit in a direction the data
have already excluded, and it costs nothing to remove.

What the refit cannot do is change any conclusion, and the reason is worth
stating because it is stronger than a sensitivity result. The zero-one-inflated
beta likelihood factorises: an observation contributes
$\mathrm{zoi}\cdot\mathrm{coi}$ if it equals 1,
$\mathrm{zoi}\cdot(1-\mathrm{coi})$ if it equals 0, and
$(1-\mathrm{zoi})\cdot\mathrm{Beta}(y \mid \mu, \phi)$ otherwise. The linear
predictor enters only the third term; `zoi` and `coi` enter only the first two,
carry no predictors, and have their own priors. The posterior therefore
separates, and the slopes, `phi`, the locality SDs and the locality correlation
matrix are estimated from the interior observations alone whatever `coi` is set
to. S6 is not a test of whether the answers survive a different `coi`; they
cannot depend on it. It is a check that this reasoning, and the code that
implements it, are both right.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-s6-identity
s6_id |>
  transmute(Response = rlab(Response), Predictor = plab(Predictor),
            `reference median` = ref_med, `S6 median` = s6_med,
            difference = d, `difference in MCSE` = z,
            `difference / posterior SD` = rel_sd) |>
  arrange(desc(`difference in MCSE`)) |>
  kt(caption = "The 21 landscape slopes under the reference fit and under S6, on the link scale. The last two columns put the difference between the two posterior medians in units of its own Monte Carlo standard error and as a percentage of the slope's posterior SD. The two runs are separate samplers over different Stan programs -- S6 has two fewer parameters -- so exact agreement is not expected and would be suspicious; agreement within a small multiple of the MCSE is what the factorisation predicts.", digits = 4)
```

Across the 21 slopes the largest difference between the two posterior medians is
`r fmt(max(abs(s6_id$d)), 4)` on the link scale, which is
**`r fmt(100 * max(s6_id$rel_sd), 1)`%** of that slope's own posterior SD and
`r fmt(max(s6_id$z), 1)` Monte Carlo standard errors. For the seven ICCs the
largest difference is `r fmt(max(abs(s6_icc_id$d)), 4)`, or
`r fmt(max(s6_icc_id$z), 1)` MCSEs. The MCSE figure is the maximum over
`r nrow(s6_id)` comparisons, so a value of three or four is the ordinary
behaviour of a maximum rather than a discrepancy; the percentage of the
posterior SD is the plainer reading, and by it the two fits agree to within a
few percent of the width of the thing being estimated.

The decisions are not merely close but identical.
`r if (s6_same_slope && s6_same_icc) sprintf("All %d slope verdicts and all %d ICC verdicts are the same under the two specifications.", nrow(s6_id), nrow(s6_icc_id)) else sprintf("%d of the %d slope verdicts and %d of the %d ICC verdicts differ, which the factorisation says should not happen and which needs explaining before either fit is used.", sum(s6_id$ref_v != s6_id$s6_v), nrow(s6_id), sum(s6_icc_id$ref_v != s6_icc_id$s6_v), nrow(s6_icc_id))`

S6 is therefore reported as the specification the data support, and the
reference fit is retained as the one every other number in this document comes
from. Nothing would change if they were exchanged, and @tbl-s6-identity is the
evidence for that claim. A reader building on this analysis should prefer the
one-inflated form, both because GIUR and the retouched perimeter cannot be zero
for a retouched tool and because it removes a parameter that has nothing to
estimate.

## Priors {#sec-priors}

::: {.barg}
Cf. BARG Step 1.C.
:::

### Why the slope prior is scaled to each response

The seven responses reach their linear predictor through three different links
(log, logit, identity), and their link-scale SDs span two orders of magnitude,
from `r fmt(min(link_sd), 3)` for `r rlab(names(which.min(link_sd)))` to
`r fmt(max(link_sd), 2)` for `r rlab(names(which.max(link_sd)))`
(@tbl-likelihood). A single nominal slope prior, `normal(0, 1)` say, is
therefore a very different statement about each of them. The clearest way to
see it is the share of the prior that falls inside that response's own ROPE,
the interval of slopes the analysis is prepared to call practically zero.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-prior-rope
pir <- data.frame(Response = rlab(resps),
                  `Link-scale SD` = round(link_sd, 3),
                  `ROPE half-width` = round(ROPE_SD * link_sd, 4),
                  `normal(0, 1)` = round(prior_in_rope(rep(1, 7)), 2),
                  `normal(0, SD_link)` = round(prior_in_rope(link_sd), 2),
                  check.names = FALSE, row.names = NULL)
kt(pir, caption = "Percentage of the slope prior lying inside the response's own ROPE, under a single unscaled normal(0, 1) and under the per-response scaling used here. One nominal specification ranges, across the seven responses, from an almost dogmatic rejection of a null effect to an almost dogmatic assertion of one; scaled to each response it is 7.97% for every one of them, by construction.")
```

The diagnostic that makes this more than an aesthetic point is the ratio of
the posterior SD to the prior SD for each slope. A ratio near 1 means the
posterior is the prior and the data contributed nothing.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ppsd
ppsd_cmp <- ppsd_s1 |>
  transmute(Response, Predictor, `normal(0, 1)` = ratio) |>
  left_join(ppsd_ref |> transmute(Response, Predictor, `normal(0, SD_link)` = ratio),
            by = c("Response", "Predictor")) |>
  mutate(Response = rlab(Response), Predictor = plab(Predictor))
kt(ppsd_cmp, caption = "Posterior SD divided by prior SD, for every slope, under an unscaled normal(0, 1) slope prior (specification S1) and under the reference prior. Values near 1 mean the data did not move the prior. The prior SD is taken from the sample_prior = 'only' draws for the reference prior and analytically for normal(0, 1).")
```

```{r}
#| label: ppsd-summary
#| echo: false
ea_old <- ppsd_cmp |> filter(Response == rlab("EdgeAngle"))
ea_new_max <- max(ea_old$`normal(0, SD_link)`)
```

Under an unscaled `normal(0, 1)` the `r rlab("EdgeAngle")` slopes have
posterior/prior SD ratios of
`r paste(fmt(sort(ea_old[["normal(0, 1)"]]), 2), collapse = ", ")`: the
posterior is very nearly the prior, so an edge-angle result read off that fit
would be mostly a restatement of the prior scale. Under the reference prior
the largest of the three is `r fmt(ea_new_max, 2)`. The unscaled specification
is kept in the sensitivity set as S1 (@sec-sensitivity), so its effect on
every quantity in the report can be read off directly.

### The reference prior

Every class that `get_prior()` lists is given an explicit prior; nothing is
left at a brms default. Two reasons. BARG Step 1.C asks for the prior to be
reported in full, and a brms default is not a reported prior --- in particular
the default intercept prior is `student_t(3, median(y), 2.5 mad(y))`, which is
a prior read off the data. And `sample_prior = "only"`, needed for the prior
predictive check of @sec-prior-pred, requires every prior to be proper.

| Class | Prior | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| `b` (slopes) | `normal(0, SD_link)` per response | one prior SD equal to the whole observed spread of that response on its own link scale: an effect as large as the response's total variation is a priori about one SD out. Puts `r fmt(prior_in_rope(link_sd)[1], 2)`% of the prior inside the ROPE for all seven. |
| `Intercept` | see below | fixed from the measurement scale, not from the sample |
| `sd` (locality) | `student_t(3, 0, 2)` | heavy-tailed half-$t$; the one class not rescaled per response, and varied in S3 and S4 |
| `sigma` | `student_t(3, 0, SD_link)` | half-$t$ scaled to the response, for the same reason as `b` |
| `phi` (zoib) | `gamma(2, 0.1)` | proper, mean 20, density zero at the origin. The brms default `gamma(0.01, 0.01)` piles mass arbitrarily close to zero, where the beta density is degenerate, and makes the prior predictive distribution unusable |
| `shape` (negbin) | `gamma(2, 0.1)` | same; the brms default `inv_gamma(0.4, 0.3)` has an extremely heavy right tail |
| `zoi`, `coi` | `beta(1, 1)` | uniform on (0, 1); this is also the brms default, stated here rather than inherited |
| `cor` (7x7) | `lkj(1)` | uniform over correlation matrices; varied in S5 |

The intercept priors are set from what a lithic analyst would have called
possible for a retouched flake tool before seeing these `r n_spec` pieces,
mapped through the link. Each is far wider than the observed spread.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-intercept-prior
kt(data.frame(
  Response = rlab(resps), Link = unname(link_lab[resp_fam]),
  Prior = unname(intercept_prior[resps]),
  `Implied 95% range on the response scale` = c(
    "6 - 100 mm", "12 - 134 mm", "GIUR 0.05 - 0.95", "0.05 - 0.95 of the perimeter",
    "3 - 143 scars", "26 - 104 degrees", "-0.9 - 6.9 generations"),
  `Observed mean` = c(sprintf("%.1f mm", mean(mod_dat$Thickness)),
                      sprintf("%.1f mm", mean(mod_dat$GMsize)),
                      sprintf("%.2f", mean(mod_dat$GIUR)),
                      sprintf("%.2f", mean(mod_dat$RLI)),
                      sprintf("%.0f", mean(mod_dat$NScar)),
                      sprintf("%.1f deg", mean(mod_dat$EdgeAngle)),
                      sprintf("%.2f", mean(mod_dat$RG))),
  check.names = FALSE),
  caption = "Intercept priors, fixed from the measurement scale rather than from the sample.")
```

One qualification attaches to the reference prior. The scale of the slope
prior and of the `sigma` prior is taken from the link-scale SD of the
response, which is a function of the data. This is a unit-setting use of the
data rather than a location-setting one: it fixes what "one unit of effect"
means without expressing any belief about where the effect lies, and it is the
standard construction behind weakly informative priors. It remains a mild
empirical-Bayes element. S1 and S2 in @sec-sensitivity vary this scale by
factors of roughly 1/8 to 2.5 and show what turns on it.

None of the priors used here is informed by previous work, because there is
none to draw on. No published posterior or meta-analytic estimate exists for
any of these seven measures in Quina assemblages; there is no prior literature
on, for instance, how edge angle varies with elevation above a channel. That
is why BARG item 5.B, sensitivity to a genuinely informed prior, has nothing
to attach to in this analysis, and the gap is itself a statement about how
little is established for these measures.

The complete prior is in Appendix A (@sec-priors-full): every row
`prior_summary()` returns, the rows it still labels `default`, the generated
Stan prior block, and the brms defaults that the explicit specification
replaced.

## Fitting and model checks {#sec-fitting}

The model was fitted in brms with the cmdstanr backend: `r mf$chains` chains
of `r format(mf$iter, big.mark = ",")` iterations, `r format(mf$ndraws, big.mark = ",")`
post-warmup draws in total, from the full run rather than a reduced pipeline
test. Ten further fits use identical settings: an intercept-only model, a
prior-only fit, a lognormal comparison for retouch generations, the six prior
variants, and one that fits a gradient slope per basin (@sec-basinx). Versions,
seeds and sampler settings are in @tbl-software.

The reference fit produced divergent transitions **`r n_div`**, iterations at
maximum treedepth **`r n_tree`**, and a largest $\hat R$ over all
`r nrow(sm_ref)` estimated parameters of **`r fmt(max(sm_ref$rhat), 4)`**. The
same diagnostics for all eleven runs, the effective sample sizes, and the Monte
Carlo standard error of every quantile the report quotes are in Appendix D
(@sec-computation).

The prior predictive draws stay inside the physically possible range of every
measure, which is what the check is asked to establish (Appendix C,
@sec-prior-pred). On the posterior side (Appendix E, @sec-post-pred), the
negative binomial captures the overdispersion of the scar count; the gaussian
likelihood for retouch generations does not capture their discreteness, which
it smooths over, and that is a real limitation of the family visible in
@fig-post-pred. The test statistics fixed in advance, including the pile-up of
GIUR and retouched-perimeter values at exactly 1, are reported against their
predictive distributions in @tbl-ppc-stats.

# Results {#sec-results}

::: {.barg}
Cf. BARG Step 4.E, which requires a decision to be accompanied by the estimate
and its interval, never reported on its own. Every decision table below
carries both.
:::

@fig-main answers both questions at a glance. The sections that follow give
the rule those answers are drawn from, then each question in turn, then how
much of the answer depends on the prior, and finally what the design cannot
settle.

```{r}
#| label: fig-main
#| fig-cap: "**A** (Q1): the locality share of link-scale variance for each response. Circles are the model with the landscape terms, triangles the intercept-only model, joined by a line. Filled circles mark responses whose 95% interval clears the 0.05 negligibility band (shaded). **B** (Q2): the 21 landscape slopes, each divided by the link-scale SD of its own response so that all seven share one axis and the ROPE is a single band at +/- 0.1. The basin slope is Huangping relative to Binchuan; height and distance are standardised, so their slopes are the change over one SD of the predictor. Rows are in the same order in both panels. Any slope whose posterior SD is still more than half its prior SD is drawn grey and hollow, because it has not been informed enough by the data to be read as an estimate."
knitr::include_graphics(FIG("barg_main.png"))
```

## The decision rule and the ROPE {#sec-decision-rule}

::: {.barg}
Cf. BARG Step 4.A.
:::

The substantive question is not only how large an effect is, but whether it is
small enough to treat as absent. An interval alone does not answer that, and
neither does a $p$-value, which can only fail to reject. The rule used here is
Kruschke's (2018) three-way decision against a region of practical
equivalence, or ROPE, meaning the band of values around the null value that
the analysis is willing to treat as no effect:

| Decision | Condition (either suffices) |
|---|---|
| **Reject the null value** | the 95% credible interval lies entirely outside the ROPE, **or** less than 2.5% of the posterior mass is inside it |
| **Accept the null value** | the 95% credible interval lies entirely inside the ROPE, **or** more than 95% of the posterior mass is inside it |
| **Undecided** | neither of the above |

An undecided verdict is a substantive outcome in its own right. It means the
data are compatible both with an effect large enough to matter and with none,
and @sec-min-rope turns that into a quantitative statement of what the design
was able to exclude.

### The ROPE and its justification {#sec-rope}

::: {.barg}
Cf. BARG Step 4.C.
:::

The ROPE half-width used in the text is 0.1 times the SD of the response on
its own link scale, so a slope is practically zero if moving a predictor by
one unit shifts the response by less than a tenth of that response's total
spread. Expressing it in link-scale SD units is what lets one number serve
seven responses on three link scales (@tbl-prior-rope).

Two qualifications attach to it. The first is that 0.1 is a convention. It is
not derived from any archaeological argument about how large a difference in
edge angle or scar count would have to be before a lithic analyst would call
it a real difference in technological behaviour. No such argument exists in
the literature for these measures, and none is constructed here.

The second is more serious. BARG asks for ROPE limits to be fixed by
theoretical and practical considerations *before the results are seen*, and
that precondition is not met in this analysis: the model had already been
fitted and inspected before this report was written. Choosing a half-width
now, with the posteriors in view, would let the bound be tuned until it
delivered a preferred verdict.

The response is therefore to report the whole curve rather than defend a
single number. The posterior mass inside the ROPE is given below as a
continuous function of the half-width, so that a reader with a defensible
bound of their own can read the answer off at it. This is the same device the
equivalence $p$-value curves of the companion analysis use, for the same
reason.

```{r}
#| label: fig-rope
#| fig-cap: "Posterior mass inside the ROPE as a function of the ROPE half-width, in link-scale SD units, for all 21 slopes. Dashed vertical line: the 0.1 half-width quoted in the text. Dotted horizontals: the 2.5% and 95% thresholds of the decision rule. A curve that has not reached 95% by a half-width the reader considers archaeologically negligible is a slope this design cannot declare absent."
knitr::include_graphics(FIG("rope_curves.png"))
```

The same information in numbers, at five half-widths, is in Appendix F
(@sec-rope-grid).

## Q1: is there technological variation between localities? {#sec-q1}

Yes, for `r nrow(present)` of the seven measures under the reference prior,
and for `r nrow(firm)` of them under every prior tried.

`r nrow(present)` responses --- `r paste(rlab(present$Response), collapse = ", ")`
--- have a 95% interval for the locality share of link-scale variance that lies
entirely above 0.05, so the null value of a negligible locality effect is
rejected under the rule of @sec-decision-rule. Their posterior medians are
`r paste(fmt(present$Median, 2), collapse = ", ")`, meaning that between
`r fmt(min(present$Median) * 100, 0)`% and `r fmt(max(present$Median) * 100, 0)`%
of the link-scale variance in those measures sits between localities rather
than within them. The remaining `r nrow(undec)` are undecided: their intervals
run from near zero to values that would be substantial, and the design does
not separate the two.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-icc-decision
icc_ref |>
  arrange(desc(P_gt_rope)) |>
  transmute(Response = rlab(Response),
            `ICC median [95% ETI]` = ci(Median, CrI_lo, CrI_hi),
            `P(ICC > 0.05)` = fmt(P_gt_rope, 3),
            Decision = Verdict) |>
  kt(caption = "Q1 decisions. The ROPE for the ICC is [0, 0.05]: a locality share of link-scale variance below 5% is treated as negligible. Unlike the slope ROPE this bound is one-sided and has a natural reading -- 5% of variance is a share no archaeological argument would build on.")
```

This is the only part of the analysis that returns a decisive answer, so how
far it survives the prior is worth setting out in detail (@tbl-sens-verdict).

`r if (nrow(firm) > 0) sprintf("For %s the decision is 'locality variation present' under every one of the seven priors.", paste(firm$Resp, collapse = " and ")) else ""`
`r if (nrow(flips) > 0) sprintf("For %s it is not: the 2.5%% limit sits so close to the 0.05 bound that %s pushes it just below, and the verdict becomes undecided (2.5%% limit %s under %s, against %s under the reference). The median barely moves -- %s against %s -- so this is a decision flipping on a boundary, not an estimate changing.", paste(unique(flip_detail$Resp), collapse = " and "), paste(unique(flip_detail$Spec), collapse = " and "), fmt(flip_detail$lo[1], 3), flip_detail$Spec[1], fmt(icc_sens$lo[icc_sens$Resp == flip_detail$Resp[1] & icc_sens$Spec == "REF"], 3), fmt(flip_detail$Median[1], 3), fmt(icc_sens$Median[icc_sens$Resp == flip_detail$Resp[1] & icc_sens$Spec == "REF"], 3)) else "No ICC decision changes under any of the seven priors."`

The safe reading is therefore the stronger and narrower one: **`r nrow(firm)`
of the seven measures carry between-locality variation that no prior in the
sensitivity set can explain away**`r if (nrow(flips) > 0) sprintf(", and %s sits on the boundary", paste(unique(flip_detail$Resp), collapse = " and ")) else ""`.

A second model provides a direct test that the landscape terms are not what
produces the between-locality variation. It was fitted with those terms
removed entirely, leaving `~ 1 + (1 |p| Locality)`. If basin, elevation and
distance were carrying the between-locality signal, dropping them would
inflate the locality variance component; equivalently, adding them to the
intercept-only model would deflate it. The comparison sidesteps the wide
intervals on the individual slopes altogether.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-icc-compare
icc_ref |> select(Response, m_ref = Median, lo_ref = CrI_lo, hi_ref = CrI_hi) |>
  left_join(icc_nol |> select(Response, m_nol = Median, lo_nol = CrI_lo, hi_nol = CrI_hi),
            by = "Response") |>
  transmute(Response = rlab(Response),
            `intercept only` = ci(m_nol, lo_nol, hi_nol, 3),
            `with landscape terms` = ci(m_ref, lo_ref, hi_ref, 3),
            `change in the median` = m_ref - m_nol,
            `as a share of the intercept-only median` = (m_ref - m_nol) / m_nol) |>
  kt(caption = "The ICC with and without the three landscape terms. A large negative change would mean the landscape terms had absorbed between-locality variance; a change near zero means they explain almost none of it.", digits = 3)
```

The three landscape terms absorb none of the between-locality variance. If
they explained it, the locality share would fall when they enter the model,
and it does not fall: the median change across the seven responses is
`r sprintf("%+.1f", med_rel * 100)`% of the intercept-only value, `r n_up` of
the seven go up and `r n_dn` go down, and the individual changes run from
`r sprintf("%+.0f", worst_j$rel * 100)`% (`r rlab(worst_j$Response)`) to
`r sprintf("%+.0f", best_j$rel * 100)`% (`r rlab(best_j$Response)`), the
largest of which starts from an intercept-only median of only
`r fmt(best_j$nol, 3)`, so that ratio is unstable rather than meaningful. The
pattern is noise scattered about zero. It is direct evidence on Q2 and it does
not depend on any single coefficient being well resolved: whatever separates
the localities, these three landscape variables are not carrying it.

## Q2: do the landscape variables explain it? {#sec-q2}

No landscape variable is shown to matter, and for most of them the study
cannot show that they do not.

Of the `r nrow(cf)` slopes, at the 0.1 SD ROPE: `r n_rej` reject the null
value, `r n_acc` accept it, and `r n_und` are undecided. The intervals are
simply too wide for the ROPE. With `r n_loc` localities carrying every
predictor, and a single binary contrast standing in for basin, that is what
the design can deliver.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-coef-decision
cf |>
  transmute(Response = rlab(Response), Predictor = plab(Predictor),
            `median [95% ETI], link scale` = ci(Median, CrI_lo, CrI_hi),
            `standardised` = ci(Std_median, Std_lo, Std_hi, 2),
            `% in ROPE` = fmt(pct_in_ROPE, 1),
            `direction certainty` = fmt(Dir_certainty, 3),
            Decision = Verdict) |>
  kt(caption = "Q2 decisions at the 0.1 SD ROPE, with the estimate and interval each rests on. 'Direction certainty' is max(P(beta > 0), P(beta < 0)): 0.5 means the posterior is split evenly about zero, 1.0 that the sign is certain.")
```

```{r}
#| label: prior-dom-readout
#| echo: false
dom <- ppsd_ref |> filter(ratio > 0.5)
```

`r if (nrow(dom) == 0) sprintf("No slope in Panel B is prior-dominated: the largest posterior/prior SD ratio over all %d is %s, so every point in the panel is an estimate the data have shaped.", nrow(ppsd_ref), fmt(max(ppsd_ref$ratio), 2)) else sprintf("Prior-dominated slopes, drawn grey and hollow in Panel B: %s. Their posteriors are still more than half as wide as their priors; they are shown for completeness and should not be interpreted.", paste(sprintf("%s ~ %s (ratio %s)", rlab(dom$Response), plab(dom$Predictor), fmt(dom$ratio, 2)), collapse = "; "))`

`r if (n_acc > 0) sprintf("What the analysis can state positively is confined to %s: %s.", if (n_acc == 1) "a single slope" else sprintf("%d slopes", n_acc), paste(sprintf("%s with %s (%s on the standardised axis, %s%% of the posterior inside the ROPE)", rlab(acc$Response), tolower(plab(acc$Predictor)), ci(acc$Std_median, acc$Std_lo, acc$Std_hi, 2), fmt(acc$pct_in_ROPE, 1)), collapse = "; ")) else "No slope can be positively called practically zero at this bound either."`

Direction certainty tells the same story from the other side. The largest
value over all `r nrow(cf)` slopes is `r fmt(max(cf$Dir_certainty), 3)`
(`r rlab(dir_max$Response[1])` ~ `r plab(dir_max$Predictor[1])`); a value of
0.5 would mean the posterior is split evenly about zero. Nothing here
approaches the near-certainty of sign that would be needed to claim a
directional landscape effect.

### What this design could have decided: the smallest acceptable ROPE {#sec-min-rope}

For each slope there is a smallest ROPE half-width at which the 95% interval
would have fitted entirely inside, namely $\max(|\text{lower}|,
|\text{upper}|)$. Anything wider than that, this design *can* declare
practically zero; anything narrower, it cannot. Translating that bound into
the response's own units turns "we could not decide" into a quantitative
statement of what the study was able to rule out.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-min-rope
cf |>
  mutate(sd_units = Min_ROPE / link_sd[Response]) |>
  arrange(sd_units) |>
  transmute(Response = rlab(Response), Predictor = plab(Predictor),
            `min ROPE, link scale` = Min_ROPE,
            `min ROPE, SD units` = sd_units,
            `min ROPE, response scale` = sprintf("+/- %s %s",
              fmt(abs(Min_ROPE_resp), 1), Min_ROPE_unit)) |>
  kt(caption = "The smallest ROPE this design could have accepted, per slope, ordered from the best-resolved to the worst. Read the last column as: an effect smaller than this, in the response's own units, is what the study can rule out; an effect larger than this it cannot.", digits = 3)
```

The one place a reader should not over-read the "undecided" label is the set
of slopes with a *small* minimum acceptable ROPE. For the three best-resolved
slopes the 95% interval is contained within
`r fmt(max(best$Min_ROPE / link_sd[best$Response]), 2)` SD, so while the
analysis will not call them zero at a tenth of an SD, it does rule out
anything larger than the following:
`r paste(sprintf("%s with %s, +/- %s %s", rlab(best$Response), tolower(plab(best$Predictor)), fmt(abs(best$Min_ROPE_resp), 0), best$Min_ROPE_unit), collapse = "; ")`.
That is a real, if modest, constraint. At the other extreme,
`r paste(sprintf("%s ~ %s", rlab(worst2$Response), plab(worst2$Predictor)), collapse = "; ")`
are effectively uninformative: their intervals span
`r fmt(max(worst2$Min_ROPE / link_sd[worst2$Response]), 1)` SD or more, and no
bound a reader would accept as negligible lies inside them.

## Are the landscape effects the same in both basins? {#sec-basinx}

::: {.barg}
Cf. BARG Step 5. A structural extension rather than a prior change.
:::

@sec-q2 asks whether the landscape explains the differences between localities
and answers no. The obvious follow-up is whether that "no" is uniform, or
whether it averages over two basins that behave differently.

The question cannot be put to the localities. All three predictors are locality
attributes, so a slope that varies by locality is not identified: within a
locality the predictor never moves, and $a_j + b_j x_j$ is a single number
however many specimens the locality holds. The basin is the finest level at
which the question can be asked, because height and distance do vary across the
localities inside each basin.

```{r}
#| label: basinx-readout
#| echo: false
bx      <- basin_slopes(gf("ref_basinx"))
bx_dif  <- bx |> filter(Quantity == "difference")
bx_bin  <- bx |> filter(Quantity == "Binchuan")
bx_hua  <- bx |> filter(Quantity == "Huangping")
bx_rej  <- bx_dif |> filter(Verdict == "reject the null value")
bx_wide <- median((bx_hua$CrI_hi - bx_hua$CrI_lo) /
                  (bx_bin$CrI_hi - bx_bin$CrI_lo))
bx_joint_h <- basin_joint_positive(gf("ref_basinx"), "zHeight")
bx_loc <- mod_dat |> distinct(Locality, Basin, Height) |>
  group_by(Basin) |> summarise(n = n(), lo = min(Height), hi = max(Height),
                               .groups = "drop")
gl <- function(b, f) bx_loc[[f]][bx_loc$Basin == b]
```

Binchuan's `r gl("Binchuan", "n")` localities span
`r gl("Binchuan", "lo")`--`r gl("Binchuan", "hi")` m above the channel and
Huangping's `r gl("Huangping", "n")` span
`r gl("Huangping", "lo")`--`r gl("Huangping", "hi")` m, so there is a gradient
inside each basin to fit a slope to.

`ref_basinx` therefore replaces the two shared gradient slopes with one of each
per basin --- `Basin * zHeight + Basin * zDistance`, the reference model
otherwise untouched. With two basins this is a fixed contrast rather than a
random slope: two groups carry no variance to estimate. Binchuan is the
reference level of the factor, so the interaction coefficient is the Huangping
slope minus the Binchuan one, and the Huangping slope itself is formed draw by
draw as their sum.

### The difference between the two basins

```{r}
#| label: tbl-basinx-diff
bx_dif |>
  transmute(Response = rlab(Response),
            Gradient = ifelse(Gradient == "zHeight", "Height", "Distance"),
            `std median` = Median, `2.5%` = CrI_lo, `97.5%` = CrI_hi,
            `% in ROPE` = pct_in_ROPE, Verdict) |>
  arrange(desc(abs(`std median`))) |>
  kt(caption = "The 14 basin contrasts: the Huangping gradient slope minus the Binchuan one, standardised by the link-scale SD of the response so that the ROPE is the same band used everywhere else in this report.")
```

Of the `r nrow(bx_dif)` contrasts, `r nrow(bx_rej)` clears the ROPE and
`r sum(bx_dif$Verdict == "undecided")` are undecided.
`r if (nrow(bx_rej) > 0) sprintf("The one that clears it is %s with %s, and its interval reaches %s at the near end -- one result out of %d comparisons, with a limit that close to zero, is what chance produces.", paste(sprintf("%s with %s", rlab(bx_rej$Response), tolower(ifelse(bx_rej$Gradient == "zHeight", "height", "distance"))), collapse = "; "), "the gradient", fmt(min(abs(bx_rej$CrI_lo)), 2), nrow(bx_dif)) else "None clears it."`
Taken one at a time, then, the contrasts do not establish that the basins
differ.

### The two basins' slopes side by side

The contrasts are not the whole picture, because a difference can be
undecided while the two slopes it separates look nothing alike.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-basinx-slopes
bx |> filter(Quantity != "difference") |>
  transmute(Response = rlab(Response),
            Gradient = ifelse(Gradient == "zHeight", "Height", "Distance"),
            Basin = Quantity,
            `std median` = Median, `2.5%` = CrI_lo, `97.5%` = CrI_hi,
            `P(> 0)` = P_positive, Verdict) |>
  arrange(Response, Gradient, Basin) |>
  kt(caption = "The gradient slopes within each basin, on the same standardised axis. Binchuan is estimated from its 21 localities and Huangping from its 5.")
```

The pattern is one-sided.
`r sum(bx_bin$Median > 0)` of the `r nrow(bx_bin)` Binchuan slopes are positive
and `r sum(bx_bin$Median < 0)` negative, scattered about zero, and
`r sum(bx_bin$excl_zero)` have an interval excluding zero. All
`r nrow(bx_hua)` Huangping slopes are positive, and `r sum(bx_hua$excl_zero)`
have an interval excluding zero. On its face that is the shape the question was
asking about: a landscape signal in one basin and none in the other.

Three things argue for reading it as a hint rather than a finding. The
Huangping intervals are `r fmt(bx_wide, 1)` times as wide as Binchuan's, so
the larger medians come with correspondingly less information behind them --- a
big point estimate with a wide interval is what a small sample looks like. The
intervals that exclude zero do so by a margin of
`r fmt(min(bx_hua$CrI_lo[bx_hua$excl_zero]), 2)` at the near end. And the
consistency of sign is weaker evidence than it appears: the posterior
probability that all `r length(resps)` Huangping height slopes are
*simultaneously* positive is **`r fmt(100 * bx_joint_h, 0)`%**, not the near
certainty that `r nrow(bx_hua)` positive medians might suggest.

The honest summary is that this design was able to ask the question and was not
able to answer it. Huangping contributes
`r gl("Huangping", "n")` localities, and the number of localities is what sets
the resolution of every landscape question in this report
(@sec-resolution-limits). Nothing here overturns the Q2 answer; it adds that the
answer was tested for basin-dependence and that the test came back undecided,
with a directional hint that a larger Huangping sample could settle.

## How far the conclusions depend on the prior {#sec-prior-dependence}

Six fits differ from the reference in exactly one prior each. Every ICC and
every slope is reported under all seven in Appendix G (@sec-sensitivity); the
summary is short.

Of the `r nrow(changed)` quantities, **`r n_changed`**
`r if (n_changed == 1) "receives" else "receive"` a different
decision under at least one of the seven priors`r if (n_changed > 0) paste0(": ", paste(changed$Quantity[changed$n_distinct_dec > 1], collapse = "; ")) else ""`.
`r if (n_changed > 0) "Those rows are the ones a reader should treat as prior-dependent; the rest are not." else "No conclusion in this report turns on the choice among the seven priors."`
The largest movement of a
posterior median across the seven priors, relative to the average width of that
quantity's own 95% interval, is
**`r fmt(worst_shift$rel[1] * 100, 1)`%** of the interval width, for
`r worst_shift$Quantity[1]`; for
`r sum(worst_shift$rel < 0.1)` of the `r nrow(worst_shift)` quantities the
movement is under a tenth of the interval width.

The quantity most exposed to the prior is the edge-angle ICC, for a reason
that is worth stating in its own right, and @sec-resolution-limits gives it.

## What this study can and cannot resolve {#sec-resolution-limits}

1. The effective sample size for Q2 is `r n_loc` localities rather than
   `r n_spec` specimens. All three predictors are locality attributes. The
   specimen count buys precision on the within-locality spread and on the
   locality offsets; it buys none on the landscape slopes. This is also why a
   slope that varies by locality cannot be fitted at all, and why the question
   has to be put to the basins instead (@sec-basinx).

2. The basin contrast is one comparison, of
   `r sum(tapply(as.character(mod_dat$Basin), mod_dat$Locality, function(x) x[1]) == "Binchuan")`
   localities against
   `r sum(tapply(as.character(mod_dat$Basin), mod_dat$Locality, function(x) x[1]) == "Huangping")`.
   Its interval will not narrow by collecting more specimens from the same
   localities.

3. The assemblages are extremely unequal. One locality supplies
   `r max(table(mod_dat$Locality))` of the `r n_spec` specimens and
   `r sum(table(mod_dat$Locality) == 1)` supply one each, which partial
   pooling handles correctly without being able to manufacture the
   information the sample does not hold.

4. The 21 correlations are weakly identified. Estimating a 7 x 7 correlation
   matrix from `r n_loc` clusters is asking a great deal, and @tbl-cor should
   be read as a description of the fitted structure rather than as a set of
   findings. S5 shows how much the LKJ concentration moves them.

5. The `sd` prior is not scaled per response, and the results show where that
   matters. The reference `student_t(3, 0, 2)` on the locality SD is left on
   one scale for all seven responses, unlike the slope prior (@sec-priors).
   For edge angle, measured in degrees with a link-scale SD of
   `r fmt(link_sd[["EdgeAngle"]], 1)`, a prior with scale 2 is restrictive;
   for log thickness, whose link-scale SD is
   `r fmt(link_sd[["Thickness"]], 2)`, it is extremely loose. The sensitivity
   analysis shows this is not hypothetical. The edge-angle ICC is
   `r ci(ea_ref$Median, ea_ref$lo, ea_ref$hi, 3)` under the reference prior
   and `r ci(ea_min$Median, ea_min$lo, ea_min$hi, 3)` under `r ea_min$Spec`,
   the largest prior-driven movement of any ICC in the set, and it happens to
   the response whose measurement scale is furthest from the prior's.
   `r ea_min$Spec` replaces the heavy-tailed half-$t$ with a prior whose tail
   dies quickly, and on a scale measured in degrees that is a strong
   statement. The refinement this calls for is the one already applied to the
   slopes: scale the locality SD prior to each response's own link-scale SD.
   That specification was not among the seven that the one-at-a-time design
   called for here, and it is the clearest open refinement of this model.
   Until it is made, the edge-angle ICC should be read as prior-sensitive.
   The measures that carry the Q1 answer are far less exposed: their
   link-scale SDs are small enough that `student_t(3, 0, 2)` is uninformative
   for them, and `r paste(firm$Resp, collapse = " and ")` hold their decision
   under all seven priors`r if (nrow(flips) > 0) sprintf(" while %s changes only because its 2.5%% limit is already touching the bound", paste(unique(flip_detail$Resp), collapse = " and ")) else ""`.

6. Retouch generations are discrete and modelled as continuous
   (@sec-post-pred), and GMsize contains Thickness (@sec-data) while the model
   assumes independent residuals across responses.

# Reproducibility {#sec-reproducibility}

::: {.barg}
Cf. BARG Step 6.
:::

## Install the software

```
R                4.5.2 or later
CmdStan          2.39.0     (install with cmdstanr::install_cmdstan())
R packages       brms, cmdstanr, posterior, bayesplot, here, readxl,
                 dplyr, tidyr, ggplot2, patchwork, knitr, quarto (CLI)
```

The backend must be cmdstanr. An rstan fit of the same model with the same
seed is a valid fit but not the same fit, and the CmdStan version above is
part of the specification: `sessionInfo()` records the R packages and not the
C++ toolchain that actually produced the draws.

## Retrieve the files

| File | What it is |
|---|---|
| `data/Quina_scraper_surface.xlsx` | specimen measurements, sheet "Quina scraper" |
| `data/Site_information.xlsx` | locality attributes: basin, height above channel, distance to channel |
| `paper/barg/barg_data.R` | builds the analysis frame; defines `link_sd`, the ROPE unit |
| `paper/barg/barg_priors.R` | all seven prior specifications, in full |
| `paper/barg/barg_models.R` | the eleven model specifications, the sampler call, the diagnostics |
| `paper/barg/barg_quantities.R` | every derived quantity: ICC, ROPE curves, HDI, MCSE, decisions |
| `paper/barg/barg_context.R` | assembles the environments the pipeline runs the above in |
| `paper/barg/barg_theme.R` | the figure style, copied from the manuscript pipeline |
| `paper/barg/barg_figures.R` | every figure |
| `paper/barg/barg_dummy_data.R` | the synthetic dataset described below |
| `paper/barg/barg_report.qmd` | this document |
| `_targets.R` | the pipeline: what depends on what, and what is rebuilt when |
| `_targets/` | the store, holding the eleven fits and the pipeline metadata |
| `paper/barg/figures/*.png` | every figure at 300 dpi |

Every table and every figure in this document is produced by the scripts in
that list: the derived quantities by `barg_quantities.R`, the figures by
`barg_figures.R`, and the tables by the code chunks of `barg_report.qmd`
itself, which reads the cached fits. Nothing is transcribed by hand, and the
code is not reproduced in the rendered document; a reader who wants it goes to
the archive.

`paper/_analysis.R` fits the same model for the two summary tables of the
supplementary information, leaving the slope prior at `normal(0, 1)` --- which
is specification S1 of @sec-sensitivity. It is not used by any of the files
above and is not modified by them.

**Archive DOI:** `<10.17605/OSF.IO/XXXXXX>` --- to be minted on OSF or Zenodo at
submission. The deposit will contain the four source files above, the
`paper/barg/` scripts, the `_targets/` store holding the fits, and the rendered HTML.

If the specimen data cannot be released, `paper/barg/barg_dummy_data.R`
generates a synthetic dataset with the same columns, types, ranges, locality
structure and missingness pattern as the real one, so that a reader can verify
that the scripts run end to end without access to the measurements. It is
simulated from the fitted model and reproduces no individual specimen.

## Run the analysis

```bash
Rscript -e "targets::tar_make()"
```

That is the whole command. The pipeline fits the eleven models, derives the
quantities, draws the figures and renders this document and the two manuscript
documents, in dependency order.

Only the fitting is expensive, and it is done once. Every later `tar_make()`
compares the stored hash of each target against its inputs and rebuilds only
what has actually changed: edit a prior in `barg_priors.R` and the eleven fits
are refitted; edit a figure in `barg_figures.R` and nothing is refitted at all.
There is no cache to delete to force a refit, and --- unlike the file-existence
cache this pipeline replaced --- no way for the document to be rendered from a
fit that no longer matches the code or the data that produced it.

`targets::tar_visnetwork()` shows the graph and what in it is out of date.
For a fast check of the plumbing that cannot disturb the real fits, the
`quick` project of `_targets.yaml` runs the same pipeline at reduced
iterations into a separate store:

```bash
TAR_PROJECT=quick Rscript -e "targets::tar_make()"
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-fit-times
r_by_fit <- if (!is.null(mf$env_by_fit))
  mf$env_by_fit[names(mf$minutes), "r_version"] else
  rep(mf$r_version, length(mf$minutes))
kt(data.frame(Fit = names(mf$minutes),
              `Wall-clock minutes` = round(unname(mf$minutes), 1),
              R = sub("^R version ", "", r_by_fit),
              check.names = FALSE),
   caption = "Time taken by each run on the machine that produced this document, and the R version that run was produced under. NA means the fit was read from cache on this run rather than resampled.", digits = 1)
```

## Session information

```{r}

cat("CmdStan version:", mf$cmdstan, "\n")
cat("Fits produced at:", format(mf$fitted_at, "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S %Z"), "\n\n")
sessionInfo()
```
