# Appendix A --- Priors in full {#sec-priors-full}

@sec-priors states the prior and the argument for scaling the slope prior to
each response. This appendix is the complete record: every row
`prior_summary()` returns, the rows it still labels `default` and why the
sampler never reaches them, the generated Stan prior block, and the brms
defaults that the explicit specification replaced.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-prior-summary
ps <- as.data.frame(prior_summary(fit_ref))[
  , c("prior", "class", "coef", "group", "resp", "dpar", "lb", "ub", "source")]
n_inherit <- sum(ps$prior == "")
n_flat    <- sum(ps$prior == "" & ps$coef == "")
ps |>
  filter(prior != "") |>
  arrange(class, resp) |>
  select(-source) |>
  kt(caption = "prior_summary(fit_ref), every non-empty row.")
```

`r n_inherit` further rows have an empty `prior` field. Every one of them
names a specific `coef` and inherits the prior of its class; they are omitted
above. Rows that specify no `coef` and are still empty --- that is, genuinely
flat priors --- number `r n_flat`. That is the condition `sample_prior = "only"`
imposes, and it is why the prior predictive draws of @sec-prior-pred exist at
all: with a flat prior anywhere, brms cannot sample from the prior. The prior
predictive fit ran, so the condition holds.

```{r}
#| label: prior-source
#| echo: false
n_user <- sum(ps$prior != "" & ps$source == "user")
n_def  <- sum(ps$prior != "" & ps$source != "user")
def_rows <- ps |> filter(prior != "", source != "user") |>
  transmute(class, resp, group, prior)
```

`r n_user` of the `r n_user + n_def` non-empty rows are marked `user`. The
remaining `r n_def` are marked `default`, which needs explaining:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-prior-default-rows
kt(def_rows, caption = "The rows prior_summary() still labels 'default'.")
```

They are not priors the sampler uses. The `sd` rows carry no `group`: they sit
one level above the `sd` + `Locality` rows that were set explicitly, and brms
takes the most specific match, so these parents are never reached. The `L` row
is brms's own restatement of the user-supplied `lkj(1)` in the Cholesky
parameterisation it actually samples in.

The authoritative record is the generated Stan program (@sec-formal) rather
than `prior_summary()`. Its prior block, extracted verbatim, is the complete
list of what was added to the log posterior:

```{r}
#| label: stan-lprior
lines <- strsplit(brms::stancode(fit_ref), "\n")[[1]]
lp    <- grep("lprior \\+=", lines)
last  <- max(lp)
while (grepl("^\\s*-", lines[last + 1])) last <- last + 1   # continuation lines
cat(paste(trimws(lines[min(lp):last]), collapse = "\n"))
```

## What the brms defaults would have been {#sec-brms-defaults}

Leaving a class at its default means inheriting a prior without reporting it,
and two of the defaults here are read off the data rather than set
independently of it. They are listed so that the cost of the explicit
specification in @sec-priors is visible.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-default-priors
gp <- brms::get_prior(fit_ref$formula, data = mod_dat)
gp <- as.data.frame(gp)
gp <- gp[gp$prior != "" & !(gp$class %in% c("b", "sd")), ]
gp |>
  transmute(Class = class, Response = ifelse(resp == "", "--", rlab(resp)),
            Group = ifelse(group == "", "--", group),
            `brms default` = prior,
            Comment = case_when(
              class == "Intercept" ~ "data-dependent: centred and scaled on the observed response",
              class == "cor"       ~ "the 7 x 7 LKJ prior",
              class == "phi"       ~ "near-improper; mass arbitrarily close to zero",
              class == "shape"     ~ "very heavy right tail",
              class %in% c("zoi", "coi") ~ "uniform on (0, 1); proper, but unstated",
              TRUE                 ~ "half-t scaled on the observed response")) |>
  kt(caption = "The brms defaults for every class other than b and sd. None of them is used by the reference fit; each was replaced by an explicit prior. The Intercept and sigma rows are read off the data, which would make them empirical priors rather than the vague priors a reader would assume.")
```

# Appendix C --- Prior predictive check {#sec-prior-pred}

::: {.barg}
Cf. BARG Step 1.E.
:::

The reference prior was refitted with `sample_prior = "only"`, so the draws
below come from the prior alone with the data unseen. The question is not
whether the simulated data look like the observed data. They should not; if
they did, the prior would be doing the data's work. The question is whether
they are physically possible: no negative thicknesses, edge angles inside the
range a goniometer can return, GIUR inside its definitional bounds, scar
counts that a flake could carry.

```{r}
#| label: fig-prior-pred
#| fig-cap: "Prior predictive distributions (grey) against the observed distribution (dark), one panel per response. Axes are clipped to the physically possible range of each measure; the table below reports what falls outside."
knitr::include_graphics(FIG("ppc_prior.png"))
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-prior-pred
ppd <- brms::posterior_predict(fit_prior, ndraws = 400)
bound <- list(Thickness = c(0, 150), GMsize = c(0, 250), GIUR = c(0, 1), RLI = c(0, 1),
              NScar = c(0, 400), EdgeAngle = c(0, 180), RG = c(0, 12))
kt(bind_rows(lapply(resps, function(r) {
  y <- as.vector(if (is.list(ppd)) ppd[[r]] else ppd[, , r])
  b <- bound[[r]]
  data.frame(Response = rlab(r),
             `physically possible range` = sprintf("%g - %g", b[1], b[2]),
             `prior-predictive median` = median(y),
             `prior-predictive 2.5%` = unname(quantile(y, 0.025)),
             `prior-predictive 97.5%` = unname(quantile(y, 0.975)),
             `% outside the possible range` = 100 * mean(y < b[1] | y > b[2]),
             check.names = FALSE)
})), caption = "Prior predictive draws against the physically possible range of each measure. GIUR and the retouched perimeter cannot leave [0, 1] under the zero-one-inflated beta, so their zero is structural.", digits = 2)
```

The prior predictive distributions are wide, deliberately so, since they
encode ignorance about the effects; but they stay inside the possible range of
every measure, and the prior passes.

## Software and settings {#sec-software}

Cf. BARG Step 2.A.

```{r}
kt(data.frame(
  Item = c("R", "brms", "Stan backend", "CmdStan", "posterior", "chains",
           "iterations per chain", "warmup per chain", "post-warmup draws",
           "seed", "adapt_delta", "max_treedepth"),
  Value = c(mf$r_version, mf$brms, mf$backend, mf$cmdstan,

  caption = "Computational settings. Chains, iterations, warmup, seed, sampler settings, brms and CmdStan are identical for all eleven runs. The R row lists every distinct R version in the cache; where it shows more than one, the cache was assembled over more than one session, and @tbl-fit-times gives the version each run was produced under. The backend is locked to cmdstanr: an rstan fit of the same model is not bit-for-bit reproducible against a cmdstanr fit, and the CmdStan version pins the C++ that sessionInfo() does not capture.")
```

All results in this report come from the full run recorded above:
`r mf$chains` chains of `r format(mf$iter, big.mark = ",")` iterations and
`r format(mf$ndraws, big.mark = ",")` post-warmup draws, rather than from a
reduced pipeline test.

## Chain convergence {#sec-convergence}

::: {.barg}
Cf. BARG Step 2.B.
:::

For the reference fit: divergent transitions **`r n_div`**, iterations at
maximum treedepth **`r n_tree`**, largest $\hat R$ over all
`r nrow(sm_ref)` estimated parameters **`r fmt(max(sm_ref$rhat), 4)`**.

Every conclusion in this report leans on more than the reference fit: the
intercept-only model carries the Q1 comparison and the five prior variants
carry the sensitivity analysis. The same diagnostics are therefore given for
all eleven runs.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-diag-all
mf$diagnostics |>
  transmute(Fit = fit, `parameters` = n_par, `max Rhat` = max_rhat,
            `min bulk ESS` = round(min_ess_bulk),
            `min tail ESS` = round(min_ess_tail),
            `divergent transitions` = divergent,
            `at max treedepth` = max_treedepth) |>
  kt(caption = sprintf("Diagnostics for all eleven runs, each of %s post-warmup draws.",
                       format(mf$ndraws, big.mark = ",")), digits = 4)
```

```{r}
#| label: div-readout
#| echo: false
d_any <- mf$diagnostics |> filter(divergent > 0)
```

`r if (nrow(d_any) == 0) "No run produced a divergent transition." else sprintf("%d of the eleven runs produced a small number of divergent transitions -- %s -- against %s draws each, that is at most %s%% of the transitions in any run. Divergences at this rate in a hierarchical model with 26 clusters and a 7 x 7 correlation matrix indicate mild curvature in the posterior near zero variance rather than a failure to explore it; the affected runs' Rhat and ESS are indistinguishable from the clean ones, and their posteriors coincide with the reference in @fig-sens-icc. They are reported rather than removed.", nrow(d_any), paste(sprintf("%s: %d", d_any$fit, d_any$divergent), collapse = ", "), format(mf$ndraws, big.mark = ","), fmt(100 * max(d_any$divergent) / mf$ndraws, 3))`

```{r}
#| label: fig-convergence
#| fig-cap: "Rhat (A) and bulk effective sample size (B) for every estimated parameter, and for the seven ICCs, which are derived quantities computed draw by draw and diagnosed like any other."
knitr::include_graphics(FIG("convergence.png"))
```

## Chain resolution {#sec-resolution}

::: {.barg}
Cf. BARG Step 2.C.
:::

Kruschke (2021) suggests an ESS of about 10,000, with the explicit
qualification that the figure is aimed at the stability of HDI limits and that
quantile-based limits are less demanding. This report is quantile-based
throughout (@sec-posterior-summary), so both things are given: the ESS, and
the Monte Carlo standard error of each quantile that is actually reported.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-convergence
#| tbl-cap: "Convergence and resolution for every parameter of the model and for the seven derived ICCs. Median and equal-tailed limits are given with their Monte Carlo standard errors; mode and HDI limits are given alongside, following the reference BARG document."
full_tbl <- bind_rows(
  bind_rows(lapply(sm_ref$variable, function(v) {
    x <- dr_ref[[v]]; s <- draw_summary(x)
    d <- sm_ref[sm_ref$variable == v, ]
    data.frame(Parameter = v, s, rhat = d$rhat,
               ess_bulk = d$ess_bulk, ess_tail = d$ess_tail)
  })),
  icc_ref |> transmute(Parameter = paste0("ICC_", Response), Median, CrI_lo, CrI_hi,
                       Mode, HDI_lo, HDI_hi, MCSE_lo, MCSE_med, MCSE_hi, SD,
                       rhat, ess_bulk, ess_tail))
full_tbl |>
  transmute(Parameter,
            `median` = Median, `2.5%` = CrI_lo, `97.5%` = CrI_hi,
            `mode` = Mode, `HDI lo` = HDI_lo, `HDI hi` = HDI_hi,
            `MCSE 2.5%` = MCSE_lo, `MCSE median` = MCSE_med, `MCSE 97.5%` = MCSE_hi,
            `Rhat` = rhat, `ESS bulk` = round(ess_bulk), `ESS tail` = round(ess_tail)) |>
  kt(caption = NULL, digits = 4)
```

```{r}
#| label: ess-summary
#| echo: false
min_bulk <- min(full_tbl$ess_bulk, na.rm = TRUE)
min_tail <- min(full_tbl$ess_tail, na.rm = TRUE)
worst    <- full_tbl$Parameter[which.min(full_tbl$ess_bulk)]
rel_all  <- with(full_tbl, MCSE_med / SD)
rel_all  <- rel_all[is.finite(rel_all)]
mcse_rel <- max(rel_all)
mcse_par <- full_tbl$Parameter[which.max(replace(with(full_tbl, MCSE_med / SD),
                                                 !is.finite(with(full_tbl, MCSE_med / SD)), -Inf))]
n_below_10k <- sum(full_tbl$ess_bulk < 10000, na.rm = TRUE)
```

Smallest bulk ESS: **`r format(round(min_bulk), big.mark = ",")`**
(`r worst`); smallest tail ESS:
**`r format(round(min_tail), big.mark = ",")`**.
`r n_below_10k` of the `r nrow(full_tbl)` quantities have a bulk ESS below
Kruschke's 10,000, so the recommendation is not met everywhere even at
`r format(mf$ndraws, big.mark = ",")` draws. What matters for a
quantile-based report is the Monte Carlo error of the quantiles themselves.
The largest MCSE of a reported median, as a fraction of that parameter's own
posterior SD, is **`r fmt(mcse_rel, 4)`** (`r mcse_par`) --- the simulation
noise in the numbers this report quotes is about
**`r format(round(1 / mcse_rel), big.mark = ",")` times smaller** than the
posterior uncertainty it describes, and the full per-parameter MCSEs are in
@tbl-convergence for anyone who wants to check a particular one.

## The checks that were specified in advance {#sec-ppc-stats}

```{r}
#| label: fig-ppc-stats
#| fig-cap: "Targeted posterior predictive statistics. Diamond: the observed value. Open circle and bar: the median and 95% interval of the same statistic over the replicated datasets. Green means the observation falls inside the interval."
knitr::include_graphics(FIG("ppc_stats.png"))
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ppc-stats
ppc_stat_tbl |>
  mutate(Response = rlab(Response),
         inside = observed >= rep_lo & observed <= rep_hi,
         verdict = ifelse(inside, "reproduced", "NOT reproduced")) |>
  transmute(Response, Statistic, observed,
            `replicated median` = rep_median, `2.5%` = rep_lo, `97.5%` = rep_hi,
            verdict) |>
  kt(caption = "Observed test statistics against their posterior predictive distributions.")
```

```{r}
#| label: ppc-readout
#| echo: false
gs <- function(r, s) ppc_stat_tbl[ppc_stat_tbl$Response == r & ppc_stat_tbl$Statistic == s, ]
rg_neg <- gs("RG", "share below zero"); rg_min <- gs("RG", "minimum")
gi_one <- gs("GIUR", "share exactly 1"); rl_one <- gs("RLI", "share exactly 1")
ns_disp <- gs("NScar", "variance / mean")
```

### Does the gaussian likelihood for retouch generations predict negative values?

The observed share of retouch-generation values below zero is
`r fmt(rg_neg$observed, 3)`; over the replicated datasets the share has median
`r fmt(rg_neg$rep_median, 3)` and 95% interval
[`r fmt(rg_neg$rep_lo, 3)`, `r fmt(rg_neg$rep_hi, 3)`]. The observed minimum
is `r fmt(rg_min$observed, 2)` against a replicated interval of
[`r fmt(rg_min$rep_lo, 2)`, `r fmt(rg_min$rep_hi, 2)`]. The gaussian's
support extends below zero, but the fitted mean sits far enough above it
relative to the residual SD that impossible values are not in practice
generated. What the gaussian does miss is the *discreteness*: retouch
generations are recorded as a small number of counted generations averaged
over at most three edges, so the observed distribution is a spike train and
the replicated one is smooth. That is visible in @fig-post-pred and is a real
limitation, though not one that biases a location parameter.

Because the check is a judgement call rather than a pass/fail, a lognormal
refit of the same response is provided as a comparison, so a reader can see
directly whether the choice of family moves the conclusions:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-rg-alt
# the RG response is on the log link in the comparison fit, so its ROPE has to
# be rebuilt from the log-scale SD rather than taken from link_sd
ls_ln  <- sd(log(mod_dat$RG))
dr_ln  <- local({ f <- gf("ref_rg_ln"); d <- as_draws_df(f); rm(f); gc(); d })
rg_alt <- bind_rows(lapply(preds, function(pp) {
  x <- dr_ln[[paste0("b_RG_", pp)]] / ls_ln
  q <- eti(x); p <- 100 * mean(abs(x) < ROPE_SD)
  data.frame(Family = "lognormal (comparison)", Predictor = plab(pp),
             `standardised median` = median(x), `2.5%` = q[1], `97.5%` = q[2],
             `% in ROPE` = p,
             Verdict = rope_verdict(q[1], q[2], p, ROPE_SD),
             check.names = FALSE, row.names = NULL)
}))
bind_rows(
  cf |> filter(Response == "RG") |>
    transmute(Family = "gaussian (reference)", Predictor = plab(Predictor),
              `standardised median` = Std_median,
              `2.5%` = Std_lo, `97.5%` = Std_hi,
              `% in ROPE` = pct_in_ROPE, Verdict),
  rg_alt) |>
  arrange(Predictor, Family) |>
  kt(caption = "Retouch generations: the reference gaussian fit against a lognormal refit of the same response. Both are shown on their own standardised axis, so the ROPE is +/- 0.1 in each case.")
```

### Do the zero-one-inflated beta fits reproduce the pile-up at 1?

For GIUR the observed share of exact ones is `r fmt(gi_one$observed, 3)`
against a replicated interval of
[`r fmt(gi_one$rep_lo, 3)`, `r fmt(gi_one$rep_hi, 3)`]; for the retouched
perimeter, `r fmt(rl_one$observed, 3)` against
[`r fmt(rl_one$rep_lo, 3)`, `r fmt(rl_one$rep_hi, 3)`]. The share of exact
zeros is 0 in the data and 0 in the replications. That is not evidence that
the model captures zero inflation; it is evidence that the zero-inflation half
of the family is estimating a probability the data have pinned at essentially
zero. See the note in @sec-likelihood.

### Is the overdispersion of the scar count captured?

The observed variance-to-mean ratio is `r fmt(ns_disp$observed, 2)`, well
above the value of 1 a Poisson would imply; the replicated interval is
[`r fmt(ns_disp$rep_lo, 2)`, `r fmt(ns_disp$rep_hi, 2)`]. The negative
binomial captures it.

## Locality-level variance and correlation structure {#sec-icc}

::: {.barg}
Cf. BARG Step 3.B, for the parameters that answer Q1.
:::

The intraclass correlation is
$\mathrm{ICC}^{(r)} = \sigma_u^{(r)2} / (\sigma_u^{(r)2} + \sigma_{\text{resid}}^{(r)2})$,
computed **draw by draw** so that it carries a full posterior. The residual
variance is taken on the link scale, and its form depends on the family:
$\sigma^2$ for the gaussian and lognormal responses;
$\log(1 + 1/\mu + 1/\text{shape})$ evaluated at the intercept for the
negative binomial; and $\psi'(\mu\phi) + \psi'((1-\mu)\phi)$ --- the
logit-scale variance of the beta component --- for the two zero-one-inflated
beta responses. For those two the ICC therefore describes the beta component
only, and ignores the inflation (@sec-likelihood).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-icc
icc_ref |>
  transmute(Response = rlab(Response), Family = unname(fam_lab[Family]),
            `locality SD` = sd_median, `SD 2.5%` = sd_lo, `SD 97.5%` = sd_hi,
            `ICC median` = Median, `2.5%` = CrI_lo, `97.5%` = CrI_hi,
            `ICC mode` = Mode, `HDI lo` = HDI_lo, `HDI hi` = HDI_hi,
            `P(ICC > 0.05)` = P_gt_rope, Rhat = rhat,
            `ESS bulk` = round(ess_bulk), Verdict) |>
  arrange(desc(`ICC median`)) |>
  kt(caption = "Locality SD and intraclass correlation, with diagnostics for the derived quantity.", digits = 3)
```

```{r}
  mutate(Response = rlab(Response), Predictor = plab(Predictor),
```

# Appendix G --- Sensitivity analysis in full {#sec-sensitivity}

::: {.barg}
Cf. BARG Step 5.
:::

Seven fits, identical in every respect except the prior, each changing one
element of the reference specification. A full factorial was not run: the
point is to attribute any change to a single choice. S1 is the unscaled
`normal(0, 1)` slope prior discussed in @sec-priors, which is also the
specification `paper/_analysis.R` uses for the main paper's summary tables
(@sec-reproducibility).

S6 belongs to a different question from the rest and is included here for
completeness rather than for its result. S1 to S5 vary how much the data are
allowed to say about a quantity the report decides on; S6 fixes `coi` at 1,
removing a parameter that no decision depends on and that the data cannot
inform, because neither GIUR nor the retouched perimeter has a zero. Its
curves in @fig-sens-icc and @fig-sens-slopes lie under the reference by
construction, for the reason set out in @sec-oneinflated, where the agreement
is quantified against Monte Carlo error rather than read off a plot.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sens-specs
kt(data.frame(
  Fit = c("REF", names(prior_specs)[-1]),
  `Prior change` = c(prior_specs$REF$label,
                     sapply(prior_specs[-1], function(x) x$label)),
  Rationale = c(prior_specs$REF$note, sapply(prior_specs[-1], function(x) x$note)),
  check.names = FALSE, row.names = NULL),
  caption = "The seven prior specifications. REF is the reference; each of S1 to S6 changes exactly one line of it.")
```

## Broad prior {#sec-5a}

::: {.barg}
Cf. BARG Step 5.A.
:::

S2 widens every slope prior by a factor of 2.5, to
`normal(0, 2.5 x SD_link)`. This is the broad prior the guideline asks for: if
the posterior barely moves when the prior is made two and a half times more
permissive, the prior is not carrying the result. S3 and S4 play the same role
for the locality SD, and S5 for the correlation matrix.

## Variations of the default priors {#sec-5c}

::: {.barg}
Cf. BARG Step 5.C.
:::

```{r}
#| label: fig-sens-icc
#| fig-cap: "Q1 under all seven priors: the cumulative posterior distribution of each ICC. The shaded band is the ICC ROPE [0, 0.05]. A curve's height where it crosses the right edge of the band is P(ICC <= 0.05)."
knitr::include_graphics(FIG("sensitivity_icc.png"))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-sens-slopes
#| fig-cap: "Q2 under all seven priors, for the slopes most exposed to the prior: the three edge-angle slopes (the response that was prior-dominated under the original specification) and the height slope of every response. Cumulative distributions on the standardised axis, with the ROPE shaded."
knitr::include_graphics(FIG("sensitivity_slopes.png"))
```

The curves are cumulative distributions rather than densities, because this
report's summaries are quantiles: a horizontal slice at 0.025 and 0.975 reads
off the interval limits directly, and the vertical distance between two curves
at the ROPE edge is the change in the quantity the decision rule uses.

BARG asks for the numbers as well as the pictures, for every parameter and not
only the plotted ones:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sens-full
#| tbl-cap: "Posterior median and 95% equal-tailed interval for every ICC and every slope, under each of the seven priors. Slopes are standardised by the link-scale SD of their response."
sens_long |>
  mutate(cell = ci(Median, lo, hi, 2)) |>
  select(Quantity, Spec, cell) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = Spec, values_from = cell) |>
  kt(caption = NULL)
```

## Do the conclusions change? {#sec-5e}

::: {.barg}
Cf. BARG Step 5.E. Some movement is inevitable, so the criterion is whether
the numbers moved enough, relative to the width of the posterior interval and
relative to the ROPE, to change a conclusion.
:::

@sec-prior-dependence gives the summary. The two tables here give the detail:
first the decision every quantity receives under every prior, then the
quantities whose posterior median moves furthest across the seven priors.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sens-verdict
kt(changed |> select(-n_distinct_dec),
   caption = "The decision each quantity receives under each prior.")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sens-shift
worst_shift |>
  transmute(Quantity,
            `range of medians` = shift,
            `mean interval width` = width,
            `shift as a share of the width` = rel) |>
  head(15) |>
  kt(caption = "The fifteen quantities whose posterior median moves most across the seven priors, as a fraction of their own interval width.", digits = 3)
```
